build_check.description: index.html and game_logic.js exist, a canvas/WebGL renderer is present, and no disallowed heavy runtime asset references are used.

requirements.description: Witness testimony contains multiple statements that can be advanced, reviewed, and pressed for extra detail. Pressing must reveal new information or change the witness response. Score 1 requires player-driven testimony navigation with visible statement index or progress. Score 0 if testimony is a single static paragraph.

Evidence can be selected or inspected and shows useful facts such as time, location, object condition, fingerprints, map position, or witness relation. Score 1 requires evidence facts to be readable and relevant to a deduction choice. Score 0 if evidence is absent or purely decorative.

Presenting the correct evidence against a contradictory statement triggers an objection, updates the testimony or case state, and visibly changes progress, credibility, or route. Score 1 requires the replay to show correct evidence chosen for a specific contradiction with observable consequence. Score 0 if evidence never affects the case.

Wrong evidence or poor choices create a visible penalty such as credibility loss, judge warning, health bar reduction, or locked-out clue. Score 1 requires a wrong action and its consequence to be observable in the replay. Score 0 if all choices succeed equally.

The game loop continues after the first contradiction: a rebuttal, new testimony phase, or second puzzle layer requires further player decisions before reaching a verdict. Score 1 requires the second layer to involve interactive deduction, not just reading. Score 0 if the case ends immediately after one correct click.

The case has at least four distinct evidence items with different roles in the logic chain, not one universal clue. Score 1 requires at least two items to matter in different deductions or testimony phases. Score 0 if evidence variety is missing.

Multiple courtroom roles appear and matter visually or mechanically: judge, witness, defense, prosecutor, clerk, defendant, or gallery. Score 1 requires staging, reactions, or role-specific behavior beyond labels. Score 0 if no courtroom roles are represented.

Testimony contains enough statements that the player must read and compare before identifying the contradiction, not a single obvious lie. Score 1 requires at least three testimony statements with only one or two being contradictable. Score 0 if testimony is trivially short.

Both successful verdict and failed or mistrial states are reachable across normal play or scenarios, each with case-specific outcome text, summary, retry, or title navigation. Score 0 if one outcome is missing entirely.

A case brief or opening phase establishes the charge, suspect, victim or location, and available evidence before testimony begins. Score 1 requires the brief to orient the player with enough context to reason about contradictions. Score 0 if the player is dropped into testimony with no context.

Normal startup shows a styled title screen with the case name, start action, and courtroom or case-file motif. Score 1 requires theme-specific scene composition with authored background, not only text labels over a flat color. Score 0 if it launches directly into raw gameplay or default UI. Score 0.5 at most for sparse or debug-like presentation.

The flow connects title or scenario to case brief, testimony, evidence interaction, objection or penalty, and verdict without restarting. Score 1 requires a playable case sequence with clear current decision state at each phase. Score 0 if transitions are missing or broken.

Dialogue, statement index, evidence details, credibility, and available actions are readable at 1280x720 without overlap or clipping. Score 1 requires the player to always be able to parse the current decision and available options. Score 0 if the player cannot determine what to do. Score 0.5 at most for cramped, overlapping, or default-control-heavy screens.

Objections, pressed statements, penalties, and verdict changes have visible feedback such as stamps, flashes, portrait reactions, screen shake, or case-board updates. Score 1 requires feedback to clearly communicate what just happened. Score 0 if important state changes silently snap with no indication.

Courtroom art direction is coherent across backgrounds, portraits, evidence cards, HUD, and result screens at a publishable vertical-slice standard. Score 1 requires consistent palette, typography, iconography, spacing, hierarchy, and authored feedback across all major screens. Score 0 if dominated by primitive shapes or raw default controls. Score 0.5 at most for sparse generic visuals or mismatched styles. Full credit may be earned with runtime-authored procedural textures, layered materials, deliberate multi-light rigs, particles, synthesized audio, or post-processing; external asset files are not required.

Evidence and case materials look like designed objects with cards, stamps, tabs, icons, or diagrams rather than plain text rows. Score 1 requires evidence presentation to feel like physical courtroom exhibits. Score 0 if evidence identity is hidden or indistinguishable.

Character portraits or witness sprites convey identity and react to courtroom events through expression changes, cut-ins, or pose shifts. Score 1 requires at least two characters with visible reactions during key moments. Score 0 if all screens are static with no character presence.

Courtroom drama is supported by animation, transitions, or timed composition: objection banners, screen flashes, text reveals, panel slides, or dramatic pauses. Score 1 requires motion and timing to reinforce the dramatic beats of the trial. Score 0 if all screens are static and flat with instant transitions.
